title: Cats Have a Secret 'ID Card' — Hidden in Their Pee!
summary:
Dogs sniff fire hydrants. Cats sniff... pee. And now scientists know why cat pee is like a secret ID card.

When a cat leaves a urine mark, other cats can tell who made it. But smells usually fade and change fast. So how do cats remember? Researchers from Japan, Germany, and Spain found the answer: 13 unusual fatty acids called BFAs.

Each cat has its own mix of these chemicals — like a fingerprint made of smell. The mix stays mostly the same for the same cat, but is different between cats. Even relatives have their own pattern.

In tests, cats sniffed the same urine less and less over time. But when a new cat's urine appeared, they got interested again. Amazingly, they still remembered old scents after months!

Cats also make a funny face called the flehmen response — mouth open, looking surprised — when they smell something new. They did it more for strange cat pee than their own.

The BFAs are semi-volatile, meaning they evaporate slowly. In samples kept at 25°C, the ID card stayed readable for at least 24 hours. So a cat's pee really does say: "I was here!"
why_it_matters: If you have a cat at home, this explains some of its weird habits — like sniffing the same spot and making that funny open-mouthed face — and it shows how science can decode messages we cannot even smell.

background_read: Cats have a much better sense of smell than people do, and they use smells to share messages with other cats without making a sound.
Many animals, including cats and dogs, leave smelly marks in their territory to tell other animals, 'I was here.'
Cats also spread their smell in other ways: they rub their cheeks and chin on furniture and people, because those spots have scent glands.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers from Japan, Germany and Spain, and the cats they tested
WHAT: The team found 13 unusual fatty acids called BFAs that give each cat its own smell 'fingerprint' in its pee
WHERE: An international study; the smelly samples were kept at 25°C during the tests
WHY: Learning how cats recognise each other's pee explains how cats communicate, and why they sniff the same spot for months and make the flehmen face

perspectives.description: People who live with cats finally have an explanation for the strange face their pet makes when sniffing new pee, and for why cats keep checking the same spots.
Scientists are excited because the fatty acids stay readable for a long time, so cats seem able to remember who visited even months later — a clever way of sending messages.
The discovery is really about one kind of chemistry in cat pee; it does not mean cats are 'talking' in words, just that smells carry simple messages like who was here.
